question: transformer attention models for language

1706.03762.caption: The figure illustrates the Transformer model architecture, consisting of an encoder stack on the left and a decoder stack on the right, both composed of $N$ repeated layers. The diagram uses colored boxes to represent functional components—such as Multi-Head Attention, Feed Forward networks, and Add & Norm layers—connected by arrows that trace the data flow from input embeddings and positional encodings to the final softmax output probabilities.

1810.04805.caption: The figure illustrates the BERT workflow, divided into two stages: "Pre-training" on the left and "Fine-Tuning" on the right. The pre-training panel shows a BERT architecture processing two masked sentences (A and B) to perform Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) and Masked Language Modeling (MLM), while the fine-tuning panel shows the same architecture applied to downstream tasks like MNLI, NER, and SQuAD using specific input pairs like question-answer pairs. A dashed arrow connects the two stages, indicating that the pre-trained parameters are used to initialize the models for fine-tuning.

2005.14165.caption: The figure uses a hierarchical diagram with brackets to illustrate the relationship between an "outer loop" of unsupervised pre-training via SGD and an "inner loop" of in-context learning. The outer loop is represented by a long purple arrow, while the inner loop consists of three separate boxes labeled "sequence #1" through "sequence #3," each containing examples of tasks (arithmetic, translation, etc.) followed by a blue vertical label for "in-context learning." The diagram conveys that pre-training enables the model to perform rapid adaptation to new tasks within a single sequence during inference.

1910.10683.caption: The figure depicts a central box labeled "T5" with several arrows pointing toward it from the left and several arrows pointing away from it to the right. The left-side boxes contain various text-based task instructions and inputs (e.g., translation, classification, and summarization), while the right-side boxes contain the corresponding text outputs. This diagram conveys the unified text-to-text framework where all tasks are treated as a sequence-to-sequence problem using the same model.

2005.11401.caption: The figure illustrates a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline consisting of a Query Encoder, a non-parametric Retriever ($p_\eta$), a Document Index, and a parametric Generator ($p_\theta$). Arrows show the flow from a query ($x$) through the MIPS search to retrieve top-$K$ documents ($z_i$), which are then passed to the generator to produce a marginalized prediction ($y$). A dashed line indicates end-to-end backpropagation through the query ($q$) and the generator parameters ($p_\theta$).

1901.02860.caption: The figure displays two diagrams of a neural network architecture with a segment length of 4, consisting of input nodes (blue circles), hidden layers (tan circles), and output nodes (white circles). The left diagram (a) shows a vanilla model where connections only exist within a single segment, while the right diagram (b) illustrates the evaluation phase where a green shaded area indicates that hidden states from the previous segment are reused as context for the current segment.

1412.6980.caption: The figure contains two line graphs comparing the training cost (negative log likelihood) of different optimization algorithms across two datasets: MNIST and IMDB. The left plot shows the training cost for AdaGrad, SGDNesterov, and Adam over 45 iterations on MNIST, while the right plot shows the training cost for Adagrad, RMSProp, SGDNesterov, and Adam (all with dropout) over 160 iterations on IMDB. In both plots, the Adam optimizer achieves a lower training cost more rapidly than the other compared methods.

2603.26380.caption: Figure 1 consists of two comparative diagrams, (a) and (b), illustrating different transformer attention mechanisms. Diagram (a) shows a stacked architecture of alternating FFN and attention layers (Sliding Window vs. Full Attention) applied uniformly to a sequence of tokens, representing a static hybrid scheme. Diagram (b) depicts a dynamic scheme where a "Router" selects between "Full Attn" and "SWA" for each individual token, resulting in a heterogeneous attention pattern across the input sequence.

2604.00965.caption: The figure displays a sequence of words ("the", "quick", "brown", "fox", "jumps", "over", "the", "lazy", "dog") at the top, with arrows pointing down to two rows of light blue boxes containing character-level tokens. These tokens represent the decomposition of the words into sub-units of at most two characters, such as "qu", "ic", and "k" for "quick," illustrating a character-based tokenization process.

2602.12192.caption: The figure displays an attention matrix where rows represent input tokens (Question, Doc1, Doc2, Doc3, [Inst]) and columns represent query-focused tokens (s1, s2, s3). Blue arrows originate from "sum" boxes at the bottom of the Question row and point toward specific attention scores in the s-columns, indicating that the retrieval and QR scores are computed by averaging attention weights along the question. The highlighted Doc2 row and s2 column signify the target gold document being evaluated.

2602.12278.caption: The figure uses colored boxes and arrows to illustrate a process where a long document is broken down into specific candidates, such as "1870 Candidates" and "October 8, 1871 Candidates." Arrows connect these candidates to yellow boxes labeled "Rank sentences and entities by scores," conveying how the AttentionRetriever identifies and ranks relevant information within a long document.

2601.03258.caption: This line graph plots Recall@50 on the y-axis against Context Tokens on the x-axis to compare two retrieval methods. It features two data series: a blue line with open circles representing "Dense + QE" and a red line with filled squares representing the proposed "QE + FlashRank (ours)." The figure conveys that while the proposed method achieves higher recall at lower token counts, the "Dense + QE" method maintains higher recall as the number of context tokens increases.

2601.00567.caption: This figure provides an overview of a framework consisting of three components: (a) concept index construction, which uses an LLM and concept extractor to map a target corpus to an academic taxonomy; (b) CCQGen, which identifies uncovered concepts from a document to generate complementary queries; and (c) CCExpand, which uses an LLM to generate concept-focused snippets for matching a concept-specific query against a latent space. The diagram uses boxes, arrows, and icons to illustrate the flow from initial index construction to query generation and final concept-focused context expansion and matching.
